Clinical Development Success Rates and Contributing Factors

Automated Pipeline Analysis
Generated April 2026

Executive Summary

Key Takeaways
  • The overall likelihood of reaching market (LOA) from Phase 1 for all developmental candidates was 15.6% (n=4,010).
  • Phase 2 remains the largest hurdle in clinical development, with only 50.6% of candidates achieving this transition (n=751).
  • The LOA from Phase 1 for non-oncology indications (24.0%) was 5-fold higher than oncology (5.3%).
  • Among drug modalities, fusion_protein achieved the highest LOA from Phase 1 at 23.7%.
  • On average, it takes 13.7 years for a Phase 1 asset to reach the market.
  • 1,886 unique sponsors contributed, with 963 (51%) having a single candidate.

Introduction

This study aimed to measure clinical drug development success rates, contributing factors to those outcomes, and timelines of clinical trials. With the goal of providing current benchmarking metrics for drug development, this study covers individual drug candidate phase transitions over 2000–2006.

A total of 4,010 clinical phase transitions were recorded and analyzed from 7,461 drug candidates across 1,886 sponsors. Phase transitions occur when a drug candidate advances into the next phase of development or is suspended by the sponsor. By calculating the number of candidates progressing to the next phase vs the total number progressing and suspended, we assessed the success rate at each of the four phases of development: Phase 1, 2, 3, and approval to market.

Having phase-by-phase data in hand, we then compared groups of diseases, drug modalities, and other attributes to generate a comprehensive analysis of drug development success.

Part 1. Phase Transition Success and Likelihood of Approval

Phase Transition Success Rates

The Phase 2 transition is clearly the main translational and limiting step from bench to bedside, as proof-of-concept is only established in 50.6% of drug candidates at this stage. Phase 2 also sees the greatest distribution between major disease areas. Within these disease areas, it is the performance of novel drug classes that has the most significant negative contribution to low overall LOA success rates.

The average timeline from Phase 1 to market was 13.7 years. This lengthy timeframe is a significant risk to investors and entrepreneurs, and speaks to the current complexities of clinical drug development. This risk is compounded by the correlation of longer timelines in certain disease areas with greater pipeline attrition rates. Disease areas with above-average LOAs tend to have the shortest development timelines, while those with below-average LOAs often carry longer development durations.

Phase-Transition Heatmaps

Major disease areas were segmented according to therapeutic convention, yielding 14 major groupings. The ordering of disease areas below is consistent with the overall likelihood of reaching market from Phase 1, which is analyzed later in the LOA section.

Success rates by disease area for Phase 1 ranged from 25.0% to 100.0%, with the average for all indications at 44.6%. Cardiovascular and the other leading disease areas were well above the average rate. With the exception of these top performers, the remainder were all within a reasonable distance from the mean.

In every disease area, Phase 2 had the lowest transition success rate of the four phases. Phase 2 success rates ranged from a high of 100.0% (Endocrine, n=4) to a low of 36.1% (Oncology, n=208). This 64 percentage-point range of disparity between major disease areas at the Phase 2 transition is the major contributor to the observed divergences in overall LOA, as discussed in the next section.

With only Endocrine (100.0%), Metabolic (76.9%), Ophthalmology (70.0%), Hematology (63.8%), Autoimmune (63.6%), Cardiovascular (60.0%), Infectious disease (58.6%), Urology (58.5%), Psychiatry (56.2%) achieving Phase 2 success rates above the overall average of 50.6%, these disease areas are also the leaders when calculating the overall LOA from Phase 1.

The lowest-performing disease groups were Gastroenterology (41.7%), Oncology (36.1%).

For Phase 3 transition success rates, Endocrine had the lowest rate at 77.8% (n=9). 7 disease group(s) ranked below the average Phase 3 transition success rate of 88.3%.

Approval to market transition success rates for the major disease areas ranged from 67.3% (Oncology) to 85.4% (Autoimmune). This distribution had the tightest range among the four phases analyzed in this report.

Interactive Bubble Heatmaps

Likelihood of Approval

One of the key measures of success used in this report is the LOA from Phase 1. The LOA is a multiplication of success rates from all four phase transitions (Phase 1→2, Phase 2→3, Phase 3→Approval, Approval→Market), a compounded probability calculation. For example, if each phase had a 50% chance of success, then the LOA from Phase 1 would be 0.5 × 0.5 × 0.5 × 0.5 = 6.25%.

Multiplying the individual phase probabilities across all disease areas, the compounded probability of progressing from Phase 1 to market reveals that only 15.6% of drug candidates (n=4,010) successfully make it to market.

As can be seen in the figure below, there is a wide range of LOAs from Phase 1. At the high end, Metabolic towers over the other disease groups at 49.3% (n=331). Metabolic therapies had an LOA from Phase 1 0.0 times higher than Endocrine, which had the lowest LOA at 0.0% (n=38).

After Metabolic, 9 other disease area(s) were above the overall average of 15.6%: Ophthalmology, Cardiovascular, Infectious disease, Neurology, Urology, Hematology, Respiratory, Others, Psychiatry.

Falling under the overall LOA of 15.6% were Gastroenterology, Oncology, Endocrine. The fact that some of these disease categories carry large n values while also having low LOA values indicates that they are significant contributors in bringing down the overall LOA.

Oncology vs Non-Oncology

Oncology drug development transitions accounted for 15% of the 4,010 total transitions. With an LOA from Phase 1 of 5.3% (n=583), Oncology had an outsized effect on the overall success rate. To further understand this contribution, we compared phase transition success rates and LOA for non-oncology candidates against oncology candidates.

The LOA from Phase 1 across non-oncology indications, 24.0% (n=3,427), was 5-fold higher than oncology alone at 5.3% (n=583). Comparing individual phase transition success rates, Oncology consistently had one of the lowest success rates for every developmental clinical transition.

In particular, there were relative differentials between Oncology and non-oncology groupings: Phase 1→Phase 2: 26.2% vs 60.8%; Phase 2→Phase 3: 36.1% vs 56.2%; Phase 3→Approval: 83.3% vs 88.8%; Approval→Market: 67.3% vs 79.2%.

Part 2. Drug Development Timelines

Drug Development Timelines

In addition to determining whether drugs are advanced or suspended at the end of a phase transition, the data can also be analyzed to yield time spent at each clinical stage, and overall drug development timelines. These are valuable metrics as there are considerable opportunity costs associated with investing in an R&D process that may take up to a decade.

Based on successful phase transitions, it took an average of 13.7 years for a drug candidate to progress from Phase 1 to market. This includes 5.2 years at Phase 1, 4.6 years at Phase 2, 3.9 years at Phase 3.

Phase duration can vary greatly according to numerous factors, such as disease area and indication, best practices of clinical trial design, and patient availability.

Disease areas with above-average LOAs tend to be associated with shorter development timelines. 11 of the disease areas fall beneath the 13.7-year average development duration. Conversely, the remaining disease areas with below-average LOAs either have durations close to the average or notably exceed it.

Ophthalmology had the shortest overall development duration at 7.5 years, while Oncology had the longest at 19.7 years.

Within Phase 1, Neurology had the longest duration at 8.3 years (average: 5.2 years).

Within Phase 2, Hematology had the longest duration at 6.7 years (average: 4.6 years).

Within Phase 3, Oncology had the longest duration at 8.3 years (average: 3.9 years).

Sponsor Concentration

A total of 1,886 unique sponsors were identified across all candidates. 963 sponsors (51%) contributed just a single candidate, while the top 10 sponsors accounted for 23% of all candidates.

The leading sponsors by candidate count were: National Cancer Institute (NCI) (479), GlaxoSmithKline (216), Pfizer (159).
